speaker: NARRATOR
text: [fresh energy, curious] In 2012, researchers looked at data on nearly thirty thousand American adults. Each of them had been asked two simple questions.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [asking you directly] How much stress do you have?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And do you believe stress is hurting your health?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [steady, a little ominous] Then the researchers waited, and looked at who had died over the following years.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [measured] People with a lot of stress who believed it was harming them had a forty-three percent higher risk of dying early.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [warmer, leaning in, lifting] But here's what nobody expected. People with just as much stress, who DIDN'T see it as harmful, didn't show that risk at all. In fact, they had some of the lowest risk in the whole study.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [slow, each phrase landing] Same pressure. Different story. Different outcome.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [honest, quicker] Now, it's one study, and it can't prove the belief itself caused it. But it raises a question worth sitting with.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [soft, intimate] What if part of what hurts us is the way we were taught to see it?
